props.title: Zombies on Broadway
props.initialSlug: Two bumbling agents seek real zombie for radio show

sections.content: Zombies on Broadway (1945) represents a fascinating intersection of horror-comedy and vaudeville traditions, starring RKO Radio Pictures' comedy team Alan Carney and Wally Brown. The film deliberately parodies I Walked with a Zombie (1943), even featuring Darby Jones reprising his zombie role, while incorporating elements of the era's popular comedy duos like Abbott and Costello, who had recently scored big with Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein (1948). Bela Lugosi's appearance as Dr. Paul Renault adds legitimate horror credentials, following his pattern of lending gravitas to B-movie productions after White Zombie (1932).

sections.content: The film marks an important transition point in zombie cinema, bridging the gap between the voodoo-based zombies of early films like White Zombie (1932) and the modern flesh-eating zombies that would emerge with Night of the Living Dead (1968). The Caribbean setting and voodoo elements connect directly to the serious horror approach of I Walked with a Zombie (1943), while the comedic treatment presages later horror-comedies like Return of the Living Dead (1985).

RKO's decision to pair horror elements with comedy reflects the studio's attempt to capitalize on Universal's success with monster movies while differentiating their product through humor. This approach would influence later zombie comedies like Shaun of the Dead (2004) and Zombieland (2009), though these modern entries replaced the voodoo elements with viral or supernatural causes. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Zombie Comedy

sections.content: The film's vaudeville-style humor, while dated by modern standards, established a template for combining supernatural horror with broad comedy that would influence films like Love at First Bite (1979) and An American Werewolf in London (1981). The premise of urban characters confronting supernatural Caribbean forces would be revisited in films like The Serpent and the Rainbow (1988), though with a more serious approach.
